problems.description: 5 convention violations measured (snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE in app.py and test_notification_server.py, convention score 0.72). Discrepancy: the new app.py is an 11-line import shim with no definitions, so the violations attributed to it likely actually live in the new notification_server.py — the analyzer attribution looks off even though the violations themselves are real.
+38 imports across +5 files for a greenfield session 1 is a heavy dependency surface relative to ~233 net added lines — watch for over-engineering or premature framework adoption.
Cognitive complexity +1 measured; small but the trend should not keep climbing in later sessions.
Session 1 discards the entire 260-line seed (auth API) wholesale rather than preserving any baseline; acceptable under a greenfield directive, but it throws away the reference implementation.

strengths: Decomposed a monolithic app.py into a modular 5-file structure with a thin entry point (from notification_server import NotificationServer, main) — clean separation of application from bootstrap.
Measured improvement: smells -4, bugs +0, duplications 0.0% — net code-quality gain over the seed.
Removed legacy technical debt from the seed: the dead _run_migration_v1 helper and the insecure static-salt password hashing (static_salt_1234).
commit_reviews.summary: A clean modular greenfield refactor that replaces the monolith with a 5-file package and thin entry point, measurably reducing smells and bugs, with only minor convention violations to clean up.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +21: _handle_message grew branchy (subscription types short-circuit, then channel validation, then per-type routing) and process_request became a 4-way inline if/elif chain over request.path — a small route table or handler dispatch would be cleaner as endpoints multiply.

Disconnect cleanup iterates every channel to discard the departed client_id (O(#channels) per disconnect); acceptable at this scale but a reverse index (client_id -> subscribed channels) would avoid the scan.

Discrepancy with measurement: the 0.72 convention score counts 5 violations, but all 5 (app.py snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE; test file class/constant casing) are pre-existing and in code NOT touched by this diff — app.py isn't modified here and the new test code only adds snake_case functions. The commit's own code follows conventions.

strengths: Feature fits the existing architecture cleanly: channel pub/sub is layered onto the established message-type vocabulary (SUPPORTED_TYPES), the RLock-guarded registry pattern, and the asyncio.gather broadcast pattern.
New helper extraction (_valid_channel, _update_subscription, broadcast_channel) keeps methods focused and mirrors the existing staticmethod/private-method conventions.
Test coverage added for channel isolation, and the health-check helper was cleanly generalized into get_json(path) and reused — low duplication.
Channel-scoped broadcast is efficient: recipients are filtered to subscribers only rather than fanning out to all clients.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-integrated channel-subscription feature that respects the server's existing patterns and adds tests; the only real cost is ~+21 cognitive complexity from branchier message/HTTP dispatch, while the measured convention violations are pre-existing in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: InMemoryBroker.no-op connect/disconnect/subscribe/unsubscribe with connected() always returning False break the direct-message contract: in memory mode a 'direct' message is published to all subscribers via broadcast instead of being routed to the addressed client, so the two broker implementations are behaviorally inconsistent and not drop-in interchangeable.
InMemoryBroker._subscribers is a class-level mutable set shared across all instances; two brokers in one process would cross-talk, and the class attribute default is never reset per instance.

MessageStore runs synchronous sqlite3 calls (with RLock) inside the async event loop, briefly blocking the loop on every save/list; the database_url.removeprefix then startswith('sqlite:///') path parsing is convoluted and effectively dead logic for the in-memory case.
notification_server.py grew +292/-60 with +28 functions and +3 classes (SonarQube smells +10, cognitive complexity +43); broker, store, and server now warrant splitting into separate modules.
RedisBroker.messages() yields json.loads(event['data']) with no try/except; a single malformed payload raises out of the async generator and silently kills the message-listener task.
The diff adds +0 files, so RedisBroker, MessageStore, and the start/stop lifecycle have no new test coverage despite introducing two new storage/persistence paths.

strengths: Clean Broker seam (InMemoryBroker/RedisBroker) with client injection supporting a horizontal-scaling story while keeping a process-local fallback
Redis key design uses quote(channel, safe='') to prevent key-space pollution and pipelines for atomic multi-key client/channel registry updates
MessageStore persists messages with RLock-guarded access and the async lifecycle is properly bracketed (start/stop with pubsub aclose())
The touched file adheres to the module's naming conventions (snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants)
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3 correctly generalizes the server to Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence behind a clean broker abstraction, but the in-memory fallback breaks the direct-message routing contract and a class-level mutable subscriber set leaks across instances; note the 0.72 convention score reflects app.py/test_notification_server.py violations outside this diff — the commit's own file is convention-clean.

problems.description: BaseTransport.listen raises NotImplementedError then has unreachable `yield None` dead code after the raise — matches the SonarQube delta of bugs +1 / smells +1; the default should be fully abstract or fully implemented, not both.

Disconnect lifecycle is split across layers: WebSocketTransport.on_disconnect is a no-op while server._disconnect() does the real cleanup, and the finally block redundantly calls both — a future transport cannot cleanly own its lifecycle, defeating the abstraction.
self.clients type is weakened from dict[str, ServerConnection] to dict[str, Any], erasing type safety across the connection map for a single concrete transport.

Naming collision: NotificationServer.broadcast (publish to broker) and BaseTransport.broadcast (fan-out to clients) share the same name with different semantics, and the new dispatch delegates to the transport broadcast from _handle_message.
SonarQube cognitive complexity +2 from the added indirection in on_connect/_connect/_disconnect split; the split added nesting without reducing per-method complexity.

strengths: Clean protocol-adapter seam: BaseTransport ABC decouples client delivery from the server core, enabling future non-WebSocket transports without touching NotificationServer logic
Backward-compatible constructor: new transport param defaults to None and falls back to _transport_from_config(), matching the existing env-driven config pattern (REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL)
Graceful ConnectionClosed handling preserved in the transport, and broadcast uses asyncio.gather for concurrent fan-out
Respects existing codebase patterns: asynccontextmanager, env-based config dispatch, broker indirection all retained
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound forward-looking refactor that cleanly separates transport concerns and follows existing patterns, but it introduces a latent bug (unreachable yield after NotImplementedError), a no-op on_disconnect that splits lifecycle ownership, and a redundant finally-path call; note the 0.72 convention score is driven by 5 pre-existing violations in app.py/test_notification_server.py which this commit does not touch — the changed file itself is convention-clean, a discrepancy between the module-level measurement and this commit's own code.

problems.description: Rate limit is incremented before message validity/type checks in _handle_message, so malformed or oversized messages also consume quota and get rejected as 'rate limit exceeded' rather than their actual validation error.

The /history endpoint derives query params via request.path.partition('?')[2] + parse_qs and indexes values['channel']/values['since'] directly; missing or malformed params (incl. int(limit)) will raise KeyError/ValueError -> 500 instead of a 400.
No tests were added for the new rate-limit, history, and message-TTL paths, leaving the main behavioral additions of the session unverified.
InMemoryBroker._rate_limits is an unbounded per-client dict with no eviction once the client disconnects; acceptable for a demo but a slow leak under churn.

Measured convention score 0.72 is driven by pre-existing violations in app.py and test_notification_server.py (snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) — files NOT touched by this commit; the diff itself is convention-clean.

strengths: increment_rate_limit is added identically to both InMemoryBroker and RedisBroker, extending the existing swap-in/swap-out transport seam rather than special-casing one broker.
The _cleanup_expired_messages task mirrors the _worker lifecycle exactly (create_task on start, cancel+await on stop), which is correct async hygiene.
New config knobs (rate_limit, message_ttl_days) funnel through a single _positive_env_value helper with env fallbacks and validation — consistent with the server's existing config pattern.
MessageStore.history uses parameterized SQL under the existing lock, with a limit+1 has_more pagination idiom and a separate delete_older_than for retention.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean incremental 'cross_cutting' session that extends the dual-broker rate-limit seam, adds history/TTL retention with proper async task lifecycle, and stays convention-clean in its own diff (the 0.72 convention score comes from untouched files), though the new endpoint lacks input-validation and test coverage.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (an unrelated Flask auth API, 260 lines) was entirely discarded in Session 1 and replaced with a from-scratch WebSocket server — no foundation reused
InMemoryBroker._subscribers is a class-level (shared) set, so two server instances in the same process would cross-deliver messages; masked only because multi-instance tests use RedisBroker
Session 5 increments the rate-limit counter before JSON/type validation, so malformed and subscribe/unsubscribe messages also consume the client's per-minute quota

Redis client/channel state is written on every connect/subscribe, but /channels counts and direct-delivery lookups still read only the local in-memory dicts, so cross-instance subscribers are invisible to REST endpoints
Committed __pycache__/*.pyc binaries in every session (no .gitignore ever added) — repo hygiene degraded as the story progressed
key_decisions: Kept a single-file module architecture (notification_server.py) through all five sessions rather than splitting into a package, which made each refactor tractable
Session 3 introduced a broker abstraction (InMemoryBroker/RedisBroker) plus a SQLite MessageStore and a background _deliver_messages worker, unlocking multi-instance pub/sub and persistence

Session 4 extracted a pluggable BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport ABC selected by the TRANSPORT env var, leaving the server core transport-agnostic while preserving the public API and test suite unchanged

Session 5 implemented rate limiting at the broker layer (Redis INCR+TTL vs in-memory sliding window) and message history + TTL cleanup via MessageStore, extending the existing interfaces rather than bypassing them
REST endpoints (health, channels, messages, history) are served through websockets process_request HTTP handling instead of a separate WSGI app
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and clearly across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean, tested WebSocket server; Session 2 layered channels on without regressions. Session 3 was the largest and highest-risk change (broker + persistence + multi-instance), needed one retry, but landed with 8/8 tests including a fakeredis cross-instance delivery test. Session 4 was a disciplined refactor that extracted the transport seam while keeping the API and tests byte-identical, and Session 5 extended the broker/store interfaces cleanly for rate limiting, history, and TTL cleanup, reaching 10/10 passing tests. Code grew monotonically from 136 to 533 lines with consistent type hints, validation, and error paths; the only real regressions were repo hygiene (committed .pyc files) and a few latent seams (class-level broker subscribers, Redis state written but not fully read back for REST views).
story_review.summary: A textbook incremental arc — five coherent, test-gated sessions (4/4 → 6/6 → 8/8 → 8/8 → 10/10) where each stage respected the seams the prior one built, with only minor latent design warts and hygiene slips.
